title: The Industrial Revolution
competency: Analyse the factors that led to the Industrial Revolution and examine its social and political results.

keywords.def: The first establishment of industrial capitalism, in Britain about 1750 (or 1780) to 1850: factories, machines and steam power.
Production concentrated in large units (factories) with many wage workers and power-driven machines.
The older system of dispersed production in many small units.
Power not from people or animals: water, wind and later steam.
An engine worked by steam from water heated by burning coal.
The middle and upper class of merchants, professionals, bankers and industrial capitalists.
The class of wage workers, especially in industry, who own only their labour power.
The late 19th-century drive of strong states for colonies and spheres of influence.

en.text: The Industrial Revolution was the first establishment of industrial capitalism, in Britain from about 1750 (or 1780) to 1850. Its heart was the change from the dispersed putting-out system to the factory system, where a capitalist owned the building, machines, power, raw materials and products, and wage workers owned only their labour. Factories produced far more at lower unit cost; by 1850 they dominated industries such as Lancashire cotton.

screens.title: The first industrial capitalism

en.text: Industry needed power greater than water and more flexible. Britain's cheap, abundant coal made steam. Thomas Newcomen's engine (first working engine usually dated 1712) only pumped water, mainly in mines; James Watt's engine of 1783–84 was more powerful and economical and drove factory machinery. Steam also powered railways: the Liverpool and Manchester railway opened in 1830, and by 1850 railways linked all important places in Britain.

screens.title: More power, anywhere
screens.ask: Factories needed more power than water wheels, and power that worked away from rivers. Britain had lots of cheap coal. What came next?
screens.after: Coal-fired steam engines drove the new machines.

screens.title: Inanimate power
paras: Machines replaced or helped work done by hand.
New machines were more numerous, complex, large and costly.
By the late 18th century they needed capitalists and factories.
They used inanimate (non-living) power.
Water and wind had been used since the Middle Ages.
Industry needed power greater and more flexible than water.
The answer was steam, from Britain's cheap, abundant coal.

screens.title: Steam engines and railways
paras: Thomas Newcomen built the first commercially useful steam engine.
His first working engine is usually dated 1712.
It could only pump water, mainly in mines.
James Watt built a better engine in 1783–84.
It was more powerful and used less fuel.
It could drive factory machinery.
From the 1780s more and more factories used steam.
The Liverpool and Manchester railway opened in 1830.
It used only steam locomotives and carried passengers and freight.
By 1850 railways linked all important places in Britain.
screens.note: The book dates Newcomen's engine "around 1705 or 1709"; the standard date is 1712.

en.text: Cheap mass production made overproduction and lack of demand the new cause of depressions, and national wealth grew but unevenly. A falling share of people farmed, yet productivity rose and fed growing towns. A richer bourgeoisie replaced the nobility as the dominant class, while a new industrial proletariat became the base of socialism. Industry and science widened the military gap between western and non-western states, steamships, railways and the telegraph tied one world economy together, and late 19th-century imperialism followed. Change became the norm.

screens.title: A new problem
screens.ask: Factories now made huge amounts of cheap cloth, but many people were poor. What new problem appeared?
opts: Overproduction: goods could not all be sold
screens.after: Poor people could not buy everything produced, so overproduction became the usual cause of depressions.

screens.title: Economic results
paras: Cheap mass production became normal.
The main problem was no longer scarcity of goods.
It became overproduction: goods were hard to sell.
Many poor people meant limited demand.
Before, depressions came from wars, epidemics or bad harvests.
Now a normal cause was overproduction from lack of effective demand.
National wealth grew, but it was very unevenly shared.

screens.title: Farms, towns and population
paras: A falling share of people lived in rural areas and farmed.
Yet farm productivity rose: fewer farmers grew more food.
Reasons: better methods, and later artificial fertilizers and pesticides.
People moved from the countryside to towns and cities.
Population grew fast despite bad living and working conditions.
More food and more jobs supported more people.

screens.title: New classes
paras: A large industrial capitalist class joined the old bourgeoisie.
The old bourgeoisie were merchants, professionals and bankers.
The bourgeoisie replaced the land-owning nobility as the dominant class.
A new industrial proletariat grew in big factories and towns.
It became the mass base for socialism and workers' parties.
Governments and ruling classes were alarmed.

screens.title: Power gap and imperialism
paras: From about 1850 industry and science were applied to armies and navies.
The power gap between western and non-western states grew.
The West wanted raw materials and markets abroad.
Steamships, railways and the telegraph (from the 1840s) tied the world together.
One integrated capitalist world economy formed.
Result: late 19th-century imperialism, a drive for colonies and spheres of influence.
The "Age of Imperialism" began around 1885 or 1890.
Finally, change itself "became the norm".

screens.text: Italy, united by 1870, invaded Ethiopia and was defeated at Adwa in 1896. Which result of the Industrial Revolution helps explain why Italy came to Africa?

notes.text: p.6: Newcomen's engine is dated "around 1705 or 1709"; the standard date of his first working engine is 1712 (developed from about 1705). The lesson teaches 1712 and mentions the book's dates.
p.5–6: the sentence on what the capitalist owned is broken as printed; the lesson reads it as "the factory, the machinery, the power unit, the raw materials and the finished products".
Unit Summary gives the end of the Industrial Revolution as 1851; the lesson text (p.5) says 1850, used here.
Activity 1.2: the unit gives no list of causes; the challenge gathers them from pp.2–6. Grade 10 causes (agricultural revolution, colonies, population) are not in this unit.
The Adwa (1896) challenge is an added Ethiopian link to imperialism.
